name: Natural law
scope: The tradition of natural law as scholarship defines it: the theory that there are objective moral standards grounded in human nature and discoverable by reason, which measure and (on the stronger versions) condition the validity of human-made positive law. It covers the Stoic and Ciceronian law of nature, Thomas Aquinas's synthesis (Summa Theologiae I-II, qq. 90-97), the early-modern natural-law jurisprudence of Grotius, Pufendorf and Locke, Blackstone's common-law naturalism, and the contemporary 'new natural law' of John Finnis. It covers the political and legal content these sources give the theory (law's moral authority, rights, just war and the law of nations, the common good, resistance to unjust rule). It excludes legal positivism and other critics (their views answer nothing), the sense of 'natural laws' as scientific regularities, and the separate ideology of natural-rights libertarianism, whose Rothbardian strand draws on the tradition. Adherents divide over whether an unjust law is invalid (conceptual naturalism, per IEP) or only defective law (Finnis and Bix), and over religious or secular grounding.

summary: Natural law holds that there are objective moral standards grounded in human nature and knowable by reason, common to all people, against which positive law is measured. On the classical and neo-classical accounts, unjust laws lack moral authority, authority exists for the common good, and basic human rights are inviolable. Property serves the common good, and war has limited just causes. Adherents differ on whether an unjust law is invalid or only defective, and on religious versus secular grounding.
